questions.challenge_mechanism: The wavelength is easy once the accelerating voltage is recognised as an energy, and the inverse problem is not: asking which voltage produces a stated ring radius requires the candidate to notice that the ring radius is proportional to the wavelength and therefore to the reciprocal square root of the voltage, so the ratio of the radii must be squared. Most attempts scale the voltage linearly with the radius, which is the natural but wrong move, and the error is large enough to matter: 1.18 times the radius needs 1.39 times the voltage.
questions.question: An electron-diffraction tube accelerates electrons from rest through a potential difference V and directs them at a thin graphite film. Electrons scattered through the correct angle reach a fluorescent screen held a distance L from the film and produce a pattern of concentric rings. The figure shows the tube, the film and the screen. The set of crystal planes that produces the first-order ring has a separation d = 2.13 x 10^-10 m, and because the angles involved are small the radius of that ring is given by r = 2L lambda / d, where lambda is the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons. The tube is operated with V = 3.00 kV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron that has been accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 3.00 kV. Give your answer in picometres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the potential difference that would be required to reduce the radius of the first-order ring from the value shown in the figure to 2.50 cm. Give your answer in kilovolts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the ring pattern provides evidence that an electron has a wave nature, and why the electrons must all have very nearly the same speed for the rings to be sharp.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The electrons are replaced by protons that have the same speed as the electrons in part (a). Discuss, with a calculation, how the ring pattern on the screen would change.

questions.answer:
(a) An electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference V gains kinetic energy $eV$, so $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = eV$ and the momentum is $p = mv = \sqrt{2meV}$ (M1).

The de Broglie wavelength is therefore

$$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 3000}}$$

The quantity under the square root is $8.75 \times 10^{-46}$, whose square root is $2.96 \times 10^{-23}$ (A1). This gives

$$\lambda = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2.96 \times 10^{-23}} = 2.24 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m} = 22.4\ \mathrm{pm}$$

The wavelength is about 22 pm, which is roughly a tenth of the spacing between the graphite planes, so diffraction is expected.

(b) The ring radius is $r = 2L\lambda/d$ and the wavelength is proportional to $V^{-1/2}$, so $r$ is proportional to $V^{-1/2}$ and therefore $V$ is proportional to $r^{-2}$ (M1).

At 3.00 kV the ring radius is $r_1 = 2 \times 0.140 \times 2.24 \times 10^{-11} / 2.13 \times 10^{-10} = 2.95 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$, which is the 2.95 cm marked on the figure (A1).

To reduce the radius to 2.50 cm, the ratio of the radii is $2.95/2.50 = 1.18$. Since the voltage varies as the inverse square of the radius,

$$V_2 = 3.00\ \mathrm{kV} \times (1.18)^2 = 3.00 \times 1.39 = 4.17\ \mathrm{kV}$$ (A1)

The voltage must be increased, not decreased, because a faster electron has a shorter wavelength and is diffracted through a smaller angle.

(c) A ring pattern is a diffraction pattern, and diffraction is a property of waves. If the electrons behaved only as particles they would travel in straight lines from the film and the screen would show a single bright spot where the undeflected beam strikes it (M1). Instead the intensity on the screen varies with angle in maxima and minima that depend on the wavelength and on the spacing of the crystal planes, which is the signature of wave interference (A1).

The rings are sharp only if every electron arrives with the same wavelength. Since $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2meV}$, the wavelength depends on the accelerating voltage, and electrons that leave the gun with slightly different kinetic energies have slightly different wavelengths. Each wavelength produces its ring at a slightly different radius, so a spread of speeds smears the ring into a broad band and eventually washes the pattern out (A1). The accelerating voltage therefore has to be stable, and the film has to be thin so that electrons lose little energy within it.

(d) The proton has the same speed as the electron, so its momentum is larger in the ratio of the masses. The de Broglie wavelength of the proton is

$$\lambda_p = \frac{h}{m_p v}$$

with $v = \sqrt{2eV/m_e} = 3.25 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$ (M1). Substituting,

$$\lambda_p = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 3.25 \times 10^{7}} = 1.22 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m}$$ (A1)

This is about $5.5 \times 10^{-4}$ of the electron wavelength, the same ratio as $m_e/m_p$. The ring radius is proportional to the wavelength, so the first-order ring would fall from 2.95 cm to

$$r_p = 2.95\ \mathrm{cm} \times 5.5 \times 10^{-4} = 1.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.016\ \mathrm{mm}$$ (A1)

which is far smaller than the beam itself. The rings would therefore not be resolved: the pattern would collapse to a single spot indistinguishable from the undeflected beam, and the experiment would give no evidence of diffraction at this speed. To see proton diffraction the protons would need a much lower speed, and hence a much lower accelerating voltage, because the wavelength has to be comparable with the plane spacing of about 0.2 nm.
questions.markscheme_notes:
Part (a): M1 for $p = \sqrt{2meV}$, A1 for the evaluated wavelength. Accept 2.2 to 2.3 x 10^-11 m, or 22 to 23 pm. A candidate who uses $E = hf$ for the electron scores nothing here; the de Broglie relation is required.

Part (b): M1 for $V$ proportional to $r^{-2}$, A1 for the ratio 2.95/2.50 or 1.18, A1 for 4.2 kV. The commonest error is to scale the voltage linearly with the radius and obtain about 2.5 kV; that scores M1 at most. Accept any answer from 4.1 to 4.3 kV.

Part (c): M1 for saying that particles alone would give one spot, A1 for diffraction or interference as the wave signature, A1 for the wavelength-spread argument. A candidate who writes only that electrons are waves without linking the pattern to wavelength and plane spacing scores M1.

Part (d): M1 for $\lambda_p = h/(m_p v)$ or for the ratio $m_e/m_p$, A1 for the wavelength about 1.2 x 10^-14 m, A1 for the conclusion that the rings are unresolvable. Accept the ratio argument in place of the absolute value if the conclusion is drawn.
questions.explanation:
The item is built around an inversion. The forward calculation, from an accelerating voltage to a de Broglie wavelength and then to a ring radius, is routine and is what most textbooks practise. Part (b) asks for the voltage that produces a stated radius, and the relation between the two is not linear. Because $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2meV}$ and $r = 2L\lambda/d$, the radius varies as $V^{-1/2}$, so the voltage varies as $r^{-2}$ and the ratio of the radii has to be squared. The natural move, scaling the voltage in proportion to the radius, gives 2.54 kV instead of 4.17 kV, and it fails in the direction that matters: it would have the candidate reduce the voltage to shrink the ring, when in fact a shorter wavelength requires a faster electron.

The figure supplies the geometry that the question needs and nothing more. The 2.95 cm marked on the screen is the value the candidate must reproduce in part (b), so the figure acts as a consistency check on the forward calculation and as the starting point for the inverse one. The distance L, the plane spacing d and the accelerating voltage are all given, and the ring itself is drawn at the radius that the calculation produces, so a candidate who obtains a very different radius can see the discrepancy. The figure is generated from the same expression the markscheme uses, which is what keeps the drawn geometry and the quoted answer from drifting apart.

Part (c) asks for the physics behind the pattern rather than the arithmetic. A ring is only evidence of wave behaviour if the alternative is stated, which is that a purely particle description predicts a single spot. The sharpness argument follows from the same relation used in part (a): the wavelength depends on the kinetic energy, so a spread of energies is a spread of wavelengths and therefore a spread of ring radii. This connects the two halves of the item and gives the candidate a reason to care that the voltage is stabilised.

Part (d) extends the wavelength relation to a different particle at the same speed rather than the same energy, which is the discriminating choice. The ratio of the wavelengths is then the inverse ratio of the masses, about 1/1836, so the proton ring is roughly a thousandth of a millimetre across and cannot be resolved. A candidate who instead gives the proton the same kinetic energy as the electron obtains a wavelength larger by $\sqrt{m_p/m_e}$, about 43 times the electron wavelength, and would predict a pattern that is easier to see rather than impossible. The two readings differ by a factor of about 79, so the item separates them cleanly.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: a real diffraction tube with a stated geometry and a stated ring radius, rather than a question that gives a voltage and asks only for a wavelength. Given and asked: the question is inverted, so the voltage has to be found from a ring radius, and the figure supplies the radius that must be reproduced. Reasoning chain: the closing part changes the particle while holding the speed fixed rather than the energy, which reverses the direction of the mass ratio and separates candidates who have understood lambda = h/p from those who have memorised a formula.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-level Physics and US AP Physics: electron diffraction through graphite, the de Broglie relation and its use with an accelerating potential difference (structure adapted; the geometry, the ring radius and the proton comparison are original)

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Scale the accelerating voltage in proportion to the ring radius, so that a radius 1.18 times smaller is obtained by a voltage 1.18 times smaller, and report about 2.5 kV
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The ring radius is proportional to the de Broglie wavelength and the wavelength varies as the inverse square root of the voltage, so the voltage varies as the inverse square of the radius and the ratio 1.18 has to be squared before it is applied
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A required voltage of about 2.5 kV instead of 4.2 kV, which also has the sign of the effect wrong because it would slow the electrons down in order to shrink the ring

verification.method: The wavelength is recomputed from h/sqrt(2meV), the ring radius from 2L*lambda/d, and the inverse voltage from the square of the radius ratio; the proton wavelength is recomputed from h/(m_p v) at the electron speed rather than at the electron energy.
solution_skeleton: Use the accelerating voltage to find the momentum from kinetic energy.
Substitute the momentum into the de Broglie relation to obtain the wavelength.
Read the ring radius and the screen distance from the figure.
Invert the ring-radius relation and square the ratio of the radii.
Explain the sharpness of the rings from the dependence of wavelength on energy.
Compare the proton and electron wavelengths at equal speed.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: E.2 Quantum physics: the photoelectric effect, the stopping potential, Einstein's photoelectric equation, the threshold frequency and the work function, and the interpretation of a graph of stopping potential against frequency
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.subtopic: Stopping potential against frequency for two metals

figure.caption: Stopping potential against frequency for two metals in the same tube.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The two lines are drawn parallel, and the standard method is to take the gradient of one of them and stop, so the parallelism is treated as a feature of the drawing rather than as a statement about the physics. The gradient is h/e and is the same for every metal; what differs is the intercept, which is the work function divided by e. A candidate who takes the gradient of each line separately and finds them equal has learned nothing, while one who reads the difference of the two intercepts has the whole of part (c).
questions.question: A student investigates the photoelectric effect using two different metal plates X and Y in the same evacuated tube. For each metal the student illuminates the plate with light of a known frequency f and measures the stopping potential V_s, the reverse potential difference just sufficient to reduce the photocurrent to zero. The figure shows the graph of V_s against f for the two metals. Both sets of readings lie on straight lines, and the two lines are parallel to each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the gradient of the lines in the figure, including its unit, and use it to obtain a value for the Planck constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the threshold frequency of each metal from the figure, and hence determine the work function of each metal in electronvolts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two lines have the same gradient, and why their intercepts on the frequency axis are different.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the stopping potential for metal X when light of frequency 9.00 x 10^14 Hz is incident on it, and state the corresponding value for metal Y.

questions.answer:
(a) The graph is a straight line for each metal, so the gradient is the same at every point. Reading from the line for metal X: at $f = 10 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ the stopping potential is about 1.8 V, and the line meets the frequency axis at about $5.5 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (M1).

$$\text{gradient} = \frac{1.8 - 0}{10 \times 10^{14} - 5.5 \times 10^{14}} = \frac{1.8}{4.5 \times 10^{14}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{V\ s}$$ (A1)

The gradient has the unit of volts per hertz, which is V s. Since $eV_s = hf - \phi$, the gradient is $h/e$, so

$$h = e \times \text{gradient} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 4.14 \times 10^{-15} = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\ s}$$ (A1)

which agrees with the accepted value.

(b) The threshold frequency is where the line meets the frequency axis, since at that frequency the stopping potential is zero and the photon energy is exactly the work function.

For metal X, $f_0 \approx 5.5 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ (A1). Its work function is

$$\phi_X = h f_0 = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 5.55 \times 10^{14} = 3.68 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J} = \frac{3.68 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 2.3\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (A1)

For metal Y, $f_0 \approx 7.7 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, giving

$$\phi_Y = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 7.72 \times 10^{14}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.2\ \mathrm{eV}$$ (A1)

(c) The photoelectric equation is $eV_s = hf - \phi$, which rearranges to

$$V_s = \frac{h}{e} f - \frac{\phi}{e}$$

The gradient of the graph is therefore $h/e$ (M1). Both graphs are measurements of the same physical process on different metals, and neither $h$ nor $e$ depends on which metal is used, so the gradient is a constant of nature and must be identical for both lines. This is why the lines are parallel (A1).

The intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency $f_0 = \phi/h$. This does depend on the metal, because the work function is the energy needed to remove an electron from that particular metal, and different metals hold their outer electrons more or less tightly (A1). Metal Y has the higher threshold frequency, so its work function is larger; more energy per photon is needed before any electron can escape. The intercept is therefore a property of the metal while the gradient is a property of nature.

(d) Using $V_s = (h/e)f - \phi/e$ with $f = 9.00 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$:

$$V_s(X) = 4.14 \times 10^{-15} \times 9.00 \times 10^{14} - 2.30 = 3.73 - 2.30 = 1.43\ \mathrm{V}$$ (M1) (A1)

For metal Y the same photon energy is available but the work function is larger by 0.90 eV, so

$$V_s(Y) = 3.73 - 3.20 = 0.53\ \mathrm{V}$$ (A1)

The difference between the two stopping potentials is exactly the difference of the work functions, 0.90 V, which is the vertical separation of the two parallel lines at that frequency.
questions.markscheme_notes:
Part (a): M1 for reading two points off a line, A1 for the gradient 4.1 x 10^-15 V s, A1 for the value of h. Accept any gradient from 3.9 to 4.4 x 10^-15 V s and any h from 6.2 to 7.0 x 10^-34 J s, since the graph must be read by eye. The unit must be given; a bare number scores M1 only.

Part (b): A1 for each threshold frequency read from the intercepts, A1 for one correct work function. Accept 5.4 to 5.6 x 10^14 Hz for X and 7.6 to 7.8 x 10^14 Hz for Y, with work functions 2.2 to 2.4 eV and 3.1 to 3.3 eV. A candidate who reads the intercepts from the wrong axis scores nothing here.

Part (c): M1 for identifying the gradient as h/e, A1 for the argument that h and e are constants and so the gradient cannot depend on the metal, A1 for the intercept as phi/h, which does depend on the metal. The second and third marks are independent; a candidate who says only that the lines are parallel because they are parallel scores nothing.

Part (d): M1 for the equation or for using the gradient, A1 for 1.43 V, A1 for 0.53 V. Accept 0.9 V for the difference as an alternative to the second value if both are shown to be consistent.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the difference between the two parameters of a straight line. The graph of stopping potential against frequency is the standard photoelectric experiment, and the usual question asks for the gradient and stops there, which teaches that the gradient is h/e without ever asking what the intercept is for. Here both parameters are examined, and the item is arranged so that the gradient is deliberately uninformative: the two lines are drawn parallel, so taking the gradient of each separately returns the same number twice and yields nothing new. The information is entirely in the intercepts.

That structure makes part (c) the discriminating part. A candidate who has understood that $V_s = (h/e)f - \phi/e$ can say immediately that the gradient is a ratio of two constants of nature and therefore cannot depend on which metal is illuminated, while the intercept is the work function of that metal divided by e and therefore must differ. A candidate who has memorised the statement that the gradient of a photoelectric graph gives h has nothing to say about why the lines are parallel, because the memorised fact does not explain the parallelism, it merely coexists with it.

The figure is load-bearing in a specific way: the axis is marked every $1 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ so that the intercepts can be read to about one decimal place, and the two lines are generated from $V_s = (h/e)f - \phi/e$ with the work functions 2.30 eV and 3.20 eV, so the intercepts sit exactly at 5.55 and 7.72 in those units and the separation of the lines at any frequency is exactly 0.90 V. A candidate who reads the intercepts carelessly obtains work functions that disagree with the difference in part (d), which is a self-check the item provides without stating it.

Part (d) is deliberately a two-mark calculation that reuses the constant from part (a). It tests whether the candidate can apply the equation rather than only interpret it, and it gives a second route to the work-function difference: the two stopping potentials differ by exactly the difference of the work functions, which is the vertical separation of the parallel lines. A candidate who obtains a difference other than 0.90 V has made an error somewhere, and the item's own numbers expose it.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: two metals measured in one tube and plotted on one set of axes, rather than a single metal plotted alone. Given and asked: the question asks for the gradient and then for the two intercepts, so the parameter that carries the physics here is the one the standard treatment omits. Reasoning chain: the explanation of the parallelism requires the equation to be rearranged rather than quoted, and the final part uses the difference of the work functions as a consistency check on the two intercepts.
provenance.resource_origin: US AP Physics 2 and UK A-level Physics: the graph of stopping potential against frequency, the gradient as h/e and the intercept as the threshold frequency (structure adapted; both work functions, the frequencies and the axis readings are original)

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Take the gradient of the line for metal X, use it to find the Planck constant, and treat the fact that the two lines are parallel as a property of the drawing rather than as a statement about the metals
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The gradient is h/e and is the same for every metal, so measuring it twice returns the same number and says nothing about why the lines are parallel; the information that separates the metals sits in the intercepts, which the gradient method never reads
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A correct Planck constant and no explanation of the parallelism, because the memorised fact that the gradient gives h does not explain why two different metals must share it

verification.method: Both lines are generated from V_s = (h/e)f - phi/e and the intercepts are recovered from phi/h independently of the plotting; the stopping potentials at 9.00 x 10^14 Hz are recomputed and their difference is checked against the difference of the work functions.
solution_skeleton: Read the gradient of one line and identify it with h/e.
Read the two intercepts on the frequency axis from the figure.
Convert each threshold frequency into a work function in electronvolts.
Rearrange the photoelectric equation to show the gradient and the intercept.
Substitute the frequency 9.00 x 10^14 Hz into the rearranged equation.
Check the difference of the two stopping potentials against the work-function difference.
